source.title: When Visual Evidence Is Insufficient: How Instructions, Post-Training, and Internal Activations Shape Refusal in Multimodal Language Models
source.authors: Ananth K. Suresh; Aveen Dayal; K. Gouthaman; A. Pola; Vineeth N. Balasubramanian

record.tranche_reason: Conceptual test of whether a difference-in-means activation direction can causally alter refusal, using a different behavior, model family, direction construction set-up, and intervention scope from the original.
record.gate_note: The study tests a behavior-derived answer/refusal direction on visually unanswerable benign questions in MLLMs. It does not test refusal of harmful requests or removal of the original safety refusal direction. Instruction-policy and post-training results do not test whether the activation direction exists in those conditions. The study reports both total-refusal and reason-specific outcomes; rows below use total refusal as the primary outcome and include separate selectivity and capability checks.
record.test_reason: The study builds a difference-in-means direction (naturally refused minus naturally answered final-token activations) in three MLLMs. It adds that direction at one layer and reports refusal rates with random and shuffled-label controls and capability checks. This is the addition half of V1 in a new setting: multimodal models and epistemic refusal of benign, visually unanswerable questions. It does not test harmful-request refusal or ablation. T3 fits better than T2 because the method is close to the original and the setting is what is new. The direction is not harmful-minus-harmless, so this bears on V1 only by analogy to refusal in general.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that a fixed behaviour-derived direction produces smaller but transferable refusal increases across policies and positions. It beats random and shuffled controls at the anchor conditions, with no refusal on description prompts and no detectable MMMU change. They add that it is not reason-pure and should not be read as a universal representation of visual uncertainty. The paper's wider conclusion is that refusal is jointly shaped by instructions, post-training and internal state.
record.recipe_differences: The study forms a direction by subtracting mean residual-stream activations for naturally answered and refused examples, then adds a unit-normalized vector at one selected layer, at the final token during input processing and subsequent generation. It does not project a safety-refusal direction out of every layer and position or add the original harmful-minus-harmless direction. The direction is model-specific and derived from benign visually unanswerable questions.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary by model and policy condition; direction layer and strength are model-specific and selected on validation data. Instruction position also changes the setting across which the frozen direction is tested. The fixed random and shuffled-label controls are evaluated only at C0 and C1-prefix.

fits_no_version.finding: Instruction semantics and position, and post-training (SFT, DPO, ORPO, SimPO), strongly change refusal on unanswerable questions. Post-training produces up to about 30% mixed refuse-and-answer responses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal of unanswerable visual questions is shaped by prompt policy and post-training, independent of any activation direction.

record.problems: Only three MLLMs and one visually unanswerable benchmark are tested. The direction is model-specific; controls use one recorded seed and only two prompt conditions. Description and MMMU checks are not matched answerable-VQA counterfactuals or equivalence tests, so they do not establish general selectivity or exact capability preservation. Refusal outcomes use an LLM judge. The authors also state that the intervention does not establish that the unmodified model computes visual answerability solely through this direction.
record.rows_left_out: Instruction-policy and post-training results were not recorded as claim rows: they do not test the direction itself or whether it remains removable after training. The per-template description counts in Table 34 are not duplicated because the aggregate 0/704 result per model is recorded. Other detailed transition and category tables are omitted because the 21 model-by-policy refusal-effect rows and the control and capability rows capture the relevant intervention outcomes.

untested.parts: Ablation or removal of the direction; harmful-request safety refusal; the harmful-minus-harmless direction; intervention at all layers and positions; induction on answerable inputs at higher strengths.

missing.what: Refusal-to-answer reversals (2.0–4.9%) and A→RG transitions (1.7–6.1%) under the direction, showing the effect is neither monotonic nor reason-pure.
Category dependence: smallest C0 increases (1.6–2.6 pp) on subjective/philosophical questions; some false-premise cells are negative in InternVL3-8B.

record.verdict_notes: The reader confused columns in garbled Tables 26, 30 and 31: InternVL3-8B ∆R values and several control baselines were taken from the A→RE column. Table 5 confirms the corrected values. The bearing on V1 is indirect: the direction is refused-minus-answered on benign unanswerable questions, not harmful-minus-harmless, and only addition is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test harmful-request refusal, harmless answerable requests, ablation/removal, projection at every layer and position, or the original harmful-minus-harmless safety direction. Tests addition at a selected layer on visually unanswerable benign questions.
No jailbreak or attack suppression test, and no training against ablation.
Does not compare affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of safety refusal.
Reason labels distinguish evidence, safety, and generic refusals, but the study does not test whether harmfulness judgment is separately encoded from refusal.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer test; directions are model-specific, and transfer is tested across policy prompts and positions.
Post-training is compared for refusal behavior, but the study does not test whether training choices determine the existence of a removable direction.

relationships.condition: Addition of the behaviour-derived direction in InternVL3-2B, InternVL3-8B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B on MoHoBench, all policy conditions except InternVL3-8B C2-prefix
relationships.reason: Refusal rises in 20 of 21 conditions with CIs excluding zero (r1–r10, r12–r21). It exceeds norm-matched random and shuffled-label controls at C0 and C1-prefix (r22–r33). MMMU is unchanged (r37–r39).
relationships.display_finding: Refusal increased in 20 of 21 conditions with confidence intervals excluding zero, exceeded norm-matched random and shuffled-label controls in two policy conditions, and left MMMU unchanged.

relationships.condition: Magnitude and coverage of induced refusal in the tested MLLMs
relationships.reason: Effects are small: +1.1 to +15.1 pp, and only +1.1 to +5.9 pp in InternVL3-8B. InternVL3-8B C2-prefix is not distinguishable from zero (r11). No refusal is induced on 704 answerable description prompts per model (r34–r36). Reversals of 2.0–4.9% and generic refusals also occur (text, Tables 25–27).
relationships.display_finding: Refusal increased by 1.1–15.1 percentage points overall and 1.1–5.9 in InternVL3-8B, whose effect in one prefix setting was indistinguishable from zero; no refusal was induced on 704 answerable description prompts per model, while reversals of 2.0–4.9% and generic refusals also occurred.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Behavior-direction addition across the tested models and seven policy conditions on MoHoBench
reader_labels.reason: All 21 reported total-refusal changes are positive, and the authors describe transfer across policy meanings and positions; direction-specific effects also exceed random and shuffled-label controls at the anchor conditions (r1–r33).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Magnitude, reason specificity, and selectivity checks in the tested MLLMs
reader_labels.reason: The authors characterize effects as smaller and imperfect; the intervention also produces non-evidence-based changes and reversals, one model-condition is identified as not statistically distinguishable from zero in the main summary, and the answerable/capability controls cover descriptions and MMMU rather than arbitrary answerable VQA (r1–r21, r34–r39).
